title: The Dharmasutra of Gautama
attributionNote: The dharma sutra of the school that bears the name of Gautama: transmitted without an author's name, and older than the metrical smritis that quote it. The library records no author for it, since the Gautama of the dharma text is not the same figure as the Gautama credited with the Nyaya sutras. GRETIL's e-text follows Ganesa Sastrin Gokhale's edition (Pune 1910, Anandashrama Sanskrit Series 61) with the variants of Stenzler's Institutes of Gautama (London 1876), and was input by Nobuyuki Watase.
description: The Gautama Dharmasūtra is the oldest of the surviving dharma sutras and the shortest: the sources of dharma, the sacraments, the duties of the student, the householder's marriage and daily rites, the law of inheritance, the king's justice and the penances that answer each transgression, all in aphorisms meant to be learned with the Veda. Its rules on initiation, food, purification and the evidence of witnesses were the seed of the legal literature that followed it.
historicalContext: Whitney, Bühler and Stenzler brought the text into European scholarship in the nineteenth century, and it was among the first Sanskrit law books to be translated; the Ānandāśrama and Stenzler editions number it differently, which is why GRETIL prints two references beside each sūtra.
availabilityNote: Complete as GRETIL publishes it: 1,017 sūtras in 28 adhyāyas, streamed from GRETIL at read time. Each passage is one sūtra, addressed as adhyāya.sūtra in the numbering of Stenzler's edition; the file prints the reference of the Ānandāśrama edition beside it, and the reader trims that apparatus from the text it shows. This is the original Sanskrit, not a translation.
